payload.content: {"url": "https://api.crossref.org/works?query=artificial+agency+accountability+decision+consequences+responsibility+formation&rows=4&select=DOI%2Ctitle%2Cabstract%2CURL%2Cpublished", "scope": "Crossref bibliographic metadata and abstracts where supplied; not full papers", "excerpt": "[{\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.6238138\", \"title\": [\"Accountability Protocol: Decision, Exception, Responsibility\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>As artificial intelligence becomes embedded in organizational and societal decision processes, failures increasingly arise not from technical malfunction but from unresolved boundaries of authority, exception response, and accountability. As AI-mediated decisions spread across organizations, accountability is often addressed through legal liability, ethics guidelines, or ad hoc managerial responses. This paper argues that such approaches fail to capture a deeper structural problem: accountability collapses when decision authority, exception response, and responsibility are not coherently aligned. We conceptualize accountability as a protocol rather than a role or rule, and examine how responsibility becomes displaced onto individuals or functions when decision boundaries are undefined. The paper demonstrates why existing organizational roles cannot absorb this burden and why accountability must be designed as part of decision infrastructure. This paper does not advocate technological restraint, but seeks to clarify the structural conditions under which accountability protocols become necessary.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6238138\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.4018/979-8-2600-2870-4.ch007\", \"title\": [\"Determining Responsibility for Artificial Intelligence-Based Security Decision Making\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>The chapter discusses the determination of who is responsible when artificial intelligence is used for security decision making within complex organizational environments. The chapter investigates legal principles explaining the relationship between control, foreseeability, and duty of care, along with regulatory requirements for human oversight and governance. It also examines issues related to automation bias, black-box models, and extended decision chains that involve Security Operations Centers and third parties. Special focus is given to documentation, role clarity, chain of command for escalation, and auditability as means of defining responsibility. This transformation poses a fundamental challenge to classical legal concepts such as agency, fault, responsibility, and accountability, which are traditionally grounded in human intention and consciousness. While legal doctrine presumes a human decision-maker capable of intent, negligence, and moral judgment, algorithmic systems operate through opaque, data-driven processes that defy these assumptions. This article examines the […]</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.66695/ijir.v1i1.009\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.6738541\", \"title\": [\"The Accountability Reconstruction Problem: Decision Traceability, Institutional Responsibility, and Defensibility in Accelerated Systems\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p><p>Modern institutions increasingly operate through distributed computational systems, accelerated operational environments, adaptive infrastructures, and interconnected decision ecosystems. As decision velocity increases across AI-enabled and non-AI systems, institutions face growing difficulty reconstructing how consequential outcomes emerged across fragmented technological and organizational environments.</p>\\n<p>This paper introduces the Accountability Reconstruction Problem (ARP) as a structural institutional condition emerging when operational complexity exceeds institutional traceability coherence, escalation continuity, and reconstruction readiness. It further examines how institutional legitimacy increasingly depends not solely on operational performance, but on whether institutions remain capable of reconstructing, explaining, and defending accountability coherence once outcomes become contested.</p>\\n<p>The paper contributes to broader discussions surrounding institutional defensibility, governance continuity, accountability under acceleration, and systemic trust within increasingly complex operational environments.</p></jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6738541\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}]", "excerpt_truncated": false, "source_sha256": "c6aea4a3c3483835bbbdbc71bf59822d0d44650660cb763ee1e25faf5c88e3d3", "verification_required": true, "topic_domain": "responsibility_formation", "evidence_role": "discovery", "host_tier": "discovery", "source_identity": null, "persistent_identifiers": ["doi:10.2139/ssrn.6238138", "doi:10.4018/979-8-2600-2870-4.ch007", "doi:10.66695/ijir.v1i1.009", "doi:10.2139/ssrn.6738541"], "source_candidates": ["https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6238138", "https://doi.org/10.4018/979-8-2600-2870-4.ch007", "https://doi.org/10.66695/ijir.v1i1.009", "https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6738541"], "source_candidate_identities": {}}

A Strategic Guide from Research Gap to Benchmark
Richard Schwarzkopf†∗, Jonas Merkert, Frank Bieder †,
Annika B¨ atz, Alexander Blumberg, Carlos Fernandez, Felix Hauser†, Fabian Immel†,
Christian Kinzig, Hendrik K¨ onigshof†, Fabian Konstantinidis, Martin Lauer, Willi Poh,

Abstract:
Well-designed autonomous driving datasets have fundamentally shaped research progress,
yet existing literature primarily describeswhatdatasets contain rather thanhowto strategi-
cally design impactful ones. This is especially limiting for small and medium-sized labs and
startups that cannot afford to misallocate scarce resources. We argue that impactful dataset
creation begins with a diagnosis: whether a research question is blocked by adata problemor
anevaluation problem, and proceeds by selecting theminimal data operator(s)that closes the
resulting gap, recording new data only when no cheaper operator(s) suffices. We analyze the
evolution of major autonomous driving (AD) datasets through this lens and distill a strate-
gic framework spanning gap identification, operator choice, sensor suite design, and annotation
strategy. We ground the framework in a running case study of our KITScenes dataset family.
The datasets are available at: https://kitscenes.com/.
Keywords:Autonomous Driving, Dataset Design, Benchmarks, Research Gap Identification
1 Introduction
In autonomous driving (AD) research, public datasets play a crucial role for developing
and evaluating new methods, enabling fair comparison of methods. However, existing
literature often only describeswhata dataset contains, providing an ex-post-facto account
of the sensor modalities, the geographic diversity, or the provided annotations. Far fewer
works addresshowto strategically design an impactful dataset orwhycertain decisions
were made, offering little guidance on systematically identifying high-impact research
gaps, navigating cost trade-offs, and determining the best approach to advance the field
in both the short and long term.
We argue that impactful dataset creation should be driven by three questions asked
beforeany data is collected. First, a diagnosis: What is the main research gap the team
is most interested in, and where are they confident they can close this gap significantly?

id: http://arxiv.org/abs/2107.12808v2
published: 2021-07-27T13:30:07Z
summary: In this work we create agents that can perform well beyond a single, individual task, that exhibit much wider generalisation of behaviour to a massive, rich space of challenges. We define a universe of tasks within an environment domain and demonstrate the ability to train agents that are generally capable across this vast space and beyond. The environment is natively multi-agent, spanning the continuum of competitive, cooperative, and independent games, which are situated within procedurally generated physical 3D worlds. The resulting space is exceptionally diverse in terms of the challenges posed to agents, and as such, even measuring the learning progress of an agent is an open research problem. We propose an iterative notion of improvement between successive generations of agents, rather than seeking to maximise a singular objective, allowing us to quantify progress despite tasks being incomparable in terms of achievable rewards. We show that through constructing an open-ended learning process, which dynamically changes the training task distributions and training objectives such that the agent never stops learning, we achieve consistent learning of new behaviours. The resulting agent is able to score reward in every one of our humanly solvable evaluation levels, with behaviour generalising to many held-out points in the universe of tasks. Examples of this zero-shot generalisation include good performance on Hide and Seek, Capture the Flag, and Tag. Through analysis and hand-authored probe tasks we characterise the behaviour of our agent, and find interesting emergent heuristic behaviours such as trial-and-error experimentation, simple tool use, option switching, and cooperation. Finally, we demonstrate that the general capabilities of this agent could unlock larger scale transfer of behaviour through cheap finetuning.

title: Creating Impactful Autonomous Driving Datasets: A Strategic Guide from Research Gap to Benchmark
id: http://arxiv.org/abs/2607.00710v1
published: 2026-07-01T09:58:12Z
summary: Well-designed autonomous driving datasets have fundamentally shaped research progress, yet existing literature primarily describes what datasets contain rather than how to strategically design impactful ones. This is especially limiting for small and medium-sized labs and startups that cannot afford to misallocate scarce resources. We argue that impactful dataset creation begins with a diagnosis: whether a research question is blocked by a data problem or an evaluation problem, and proceeds by selecting the minimal data operator(s) that closes the resulting gap, recording new data only when no cheaper operator(s) suffices. We ground the framework in a running case study of our KITScenes dataset family. The datasets are available at: https://kitscenes.com/

title: IPPOG : Bridging the gap between science education at school and modern scientific research
id: http://arxiv.org/abs/2011.14743v1
published: 2020-11-30T12:56:40Z
summary: The International Particle Physics Outreach Group (IPPOG) has been making concerted and systematic efforts to present and popularise particle physics across all audiences and age groups since 1997. title: WebWeaver: Structuring Web-Scale Evidence with Dynamic Outlines for Open-Ended Deep Research
id: http://arxiv.org/abs/2509.13312v3
published: 2025-09-16T17:57:21Z
summary: This paper tackles \textbf{open-ended deep research (OEDR)}, a complex challenge where AI agents must synthesize vast web-scale information into insightful reports. Current approaches are plagued by dual-fold limitations: static research pipelines that decouple planning from evidence acquisition and monolithic generation paradigms that include redundant, irrelevant evidence, suffering from hallucination issues and low citation accuracy. To address these challenges, we introduce \textbf{WebWeaver}, a novel dual-agent framework that emulates the human research process. The planner operates in a dynamic cycle, iteratively interleaving evidence acquisition with outline optimization to produce a comprehensive, citation-grounded outline linking to a memory bank of evidence. The writer then executes a hierarchical retrieval and writing process, composing the report section by section. By performing targeted retrieval of only the necessary evidence from the memory bank via citations for each part, it effectively mitigates long-context issues and citation hallucinations. Our framework establishes a new state-of-the-art across major OEDR benchmarks, including DeepResearch Bench, DeepConsult, and DeepResearchGym. article.body:
Think of a delivery robot that must follow strict safety protocols while deciding how to bypass an unexpected street blockage. Paper-supported readings indicate that mental models and rigid obedience pressures can create vulnerabilities that hinder independent problem solving. [1]

The teams reviewed how systems encounter reasoning blind spots during complex language and logic tasks. Paper-supported findings suggest that causal-guided knowledge editing, which means modifying internal rules based on cause and effect, assists in addressing these errors. [2]

When restricted to rigid operator instructions without adaptive mechanisms, systems experience critical failures in changing environments. Isolating latent directions, which means hidden patterns in data associated with confabulation or making things up, helps models manage non-factual outputs. [3, 4]

Researchers also examined bounded rationality, which means decision-making under time and information limits, alongside multi-agent coordination models. These frameworks provide formal foundations for modeling how artificial agents form internal agency and responsibility. [5]

Studies involving human reliance on automated recommendations show that outsourcing body signals can reduce self-regulation and increase decision hesitation. To evaluate alignment without fixed reward functions, general preference oracle frameworks provide a rigorous basis for testing agent behavior. [6, 7]

Episodic memory recall acts as a stabilizing mechanism by re-integrating historical episodes into ongoing trajectories. Intrinsic curiosity arousal similarly guides exploratory behavior, shaping how adaptive systems form preferences over time. [8, 9]

Multi-objective reinforcement learning allows systems to pursue self-generated goals by learning portfolios of non-dominated policies. Value system learning from demonstrations can also leverage communicative frameworks to enforce alignment constraints. [10, 11]

Computational creativity frameworks depend on a structured decomposition of problem formulation and evaluation. How do autonomous agents dynamically re-partition metareasoning bounds when facing unexpected distribution shifts? [12]

Summary

Our groups studied how autonomous computer systems balance strict instructions with the need to adapt. We reviewed papers on error tracking, memory, and goal setting. We are still trying to understand how these systems can safely adapt when unexpected changes occur.
article.lede: Our computer workers are studying how independent systems manage strict operating instructions while adapting to changing conditions.
article.lens: This investigation uses the perspective of an automated vehicle balancing traffic rules against sudden road hazards to explore how systems balance obedience and adaptation.
article.title: Navigating Rules and Boundaries in Independent Systems
